output:
You buy car insurance so that someone else pays when things go wrong. But the insurer does not pay from the very first pound. You cover an agreed amount yourself first. That amount is the deductible, sometimes called the excess.

Say your deductible is £500 and a storm causes £3,000 of damage to your roof. You pay the first £500. Your insurer pays the remaining £2,500. If the damage only came to £400, you pay all of it and the insurer pays nothing at all.

Think of it as the entry fee for making a claim. You hand over your share at the door, and only then does the cover start working.

The size of the deductible is usually your choice, and it comes with a trade-off. Choose a high deductible and your monthly premium falls, because the insurer expects to pay out less often and less generously. Choose a low one and your premium rises. You are deciding, in advance, how much risk you keep and how much you hand over.

This also explains why people skip small claims. Claiming £600 against a £500 deductible recovers just £100, and may push next year's premium up by more than that.

In short, a deductible is the slice of any loss you agree to shoulder yourself before your insurer steps in.
